analysts: GAM Research — Oil, Gas & Consumable Fuels

cover.headline: The most marketing-heavy OMC, priced for a normal year: SELL
cover.lead: HPCL refines ~26 MMT a year but sells ~51 MMT through 25,098 fuel stations and India's second-largest LPG network, so it gains most when retail prices are generous and loses most when the Government holds them. It earned ₹18,047 cr in FY26, then lost ₹12,265 cr in Q1FY27 as crude passed US$100/bbl. At ₹350.4 the stock is 7.2x our FY28E EPS of ₹48.9 and 1.1x book, and 4.4x FY28E EBITDA after taking out its investments: about what its own history pays (median 3.9x since Apr-2021, trough years left out), while oil marketers and refiners trade 14.3% below their five-year medians. On 3.5x Sep-28E EBITDA of ₹24,148 cr, less net debt, plus MRPL and Oil India at market less 20% and the HRRL loan, we get **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with SELL.** The street (median ₹420; ₹424 after Q1) uses 6x standalone EBITDA. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}: debt makes the equity a geared bet on margins.

arguments.h: A marketing company with refineries attached
arguments.p: HPCL's own refineries cover only about half of its sales; the rest comes from its JV refineries (HMEL, MRPL, now HRRL) and other refiners. EBITDA per tonne sold was −₹1,655 in FY23, ₹3,301 in FY25 and ₹5,956 in FY26: a range set by Delhi's pricing and global cracks, not by HPCL. Q1FY27 marketing under-recoveries topped ₹26,000 cr. We forecast ₹700/t in FY27E and ₹4,300-4,500/t after, the FY22-26 average without the FY23 loss year.

arguments.h: HRRL is finally running, but it is a geared bet
arguments.p: The 9 MMTPA Barmer refinery-cum-petrochemical complex started commercial operation in end-June/July 2026, ~4 years late, at ₹79,459 cr (from ₹43,129 cr). HPCL owns 74% and has put in ₹18,916 cr; HRRL's ~₹53,000 cr of debt is off HPCL's balance sheet. We carry it at book (₹18,478 cr, ~₹87 a share); the street ranges from nothing (BOB, Emkay) to 0.8x invested (MOSL).

arguments.h: The balance sheet swings with crude
arguments.p: Net debt after counting every investment fell to ~₹27,800 cr at Mar-26, then gross debt jumped ₹25,000 cr to ₹72,600 cr in Q1FY27. A ₹16,410 cr negative LPG buffer is not on the balance sheet. With ~₹31,537 cr of net debt at Mar-27E against a market value of ₹74,552 cr, each 0.5x on the multiple moves the value by ~₹57 a share.

arguments.h: Valuation: we follow the street's method, not its multiple
arguments.p: The street pays 6x standalone EBITDA plus investments. HPCL's own history says the market pays ~3.9x for the business once investments are taken out (4.9x if they are left in), and the sector trades below its averages. 3.5x gives {{dcf.tp|inr}}. Cross-checks: P/E ₹235; DCF ₹586 (only if a 4% EBITDA margin held for a decade without another squeeze).

flags.k: Accounting (inventory losses, LPG buffer off balance sheet)

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): marketing margins after the price rises, LPG losses (~₹490/cylinder in July), inventory effects, debt after the Q1 jump.
HRRL ramp-up: ~50-60% in Q2FY27, 80-85% in Q3, full refinery capacity in Q4FY27; petrochemicals by end-FY27.
Stable running of the Vizag residue upgrade (expected Q2-Q3FY27; ~US$2.5/bbl on Vizag's GRM per BOB).
Government decisions: retail prices, SAED and export duties, compensation for the ₹16,410 cr negative LPG buffer.
Crude and the Strait of Hormuz: each US$10/bbl moves HPCL's working capital and its marketing margin.

sections.title: A fuel and LPG marketer with two refineries, three JV refineries and an ONGC parent

blocks.p: Hindustan Petroleum Corporation (HPCL) is a Maharatna public-sector company controlled by ONGC (54.90%), which is itself controlled by the Government. It owns two refineries, Mumbai (9.5 MMTPA) and Visakhapatnam (15 MMTPA after its modernisation), which processed a record 26.04 MMT in FY26 (106.3% utilisation; GRM US$8.79/bbl). It sold 51.45 MMT through 25,098 fuel stations (1,353 added in FY26), 6,389 LPG distributors (9.41 MMT of LPG, India's second-largest LPG marketer), aviation (1.16 MMT), lubricants (686 TMT) and direct sales to industry (5.9 MMT), and moved 25.54 MMT through its pipelines.

blocks.p: This mix is the key to HPCL. Refining earns the global crack; marketing earns the gap between the retail price and the refinery-gate price, which in practice is decided with the Government. HPCL markets about twice what it refines, so its profits lean on marketing more than IOC's or BPCL's. When crude falls and prices are held (FY24) it does very well; when crude spikes and prices are held (FY23, Q1FY27) it loses more than its peers. HRRL changes the mix only partly: its refining margin is earned inside a joint venture and reaches HPCL as a 74% share of profit, while HPCL keeps the marketing of its products.

sections.title: A growing fuel market with administered prices, hit again by the 2026 Gulf war

blocks.p: Three state oil marketing companies (IOC, BPCL, HPCL) sell most of India's petrol, diesel and LPG at prices set in practice with the Government; Reliance and Nayara are export-oriented private refiners with smaller retail networks; MRPL (ONGC group) and CPCL (IOC group) are standalone refiners. HPCL is the smallest refiner of the three OMCs but has the third-largest retail network (25,098 outlets) and is the second-largest LPG marketer (ar26).

US-Iran conflict from end-Feb 2026: Strait of Hormuz disrupted; Brent averaged ~US$105/bbl in Q1FY27 vs US$76 in Q4FY26 (BOB); diesel cracks ~US$50/bbl and petrol ~US$25 (BOB). The Government cut excise (SAED) on petrol and diesel by ₹10/litre in Mar-2026, re-imposed export duties, and allowed retail price rises in tranches from May. The three OMCs lost money on fuel marketing in Q1FY27; refiners and HPCL's refining arm earned record cracks, part of which the export duty took away.

Petrol and diesel prices are formally deregulated but were held for long stretches, including through the 2026 Gulf war; household LPG is sold below cost and compensated case by case (₹7,920 cr for HPCL conveyed in Oct-2025 for under-recoveries to Mar-2026). Losses on LPG not yet compensated sit off the balance sheet in a 'negative buffer' (₹16,410 cr for HPCL at Jun-2026).

blocks.callout: **So what:** demand growth (3-5% a year) is not HPCL's problem; who bears the cost of high crude is. In 2022 and again in 2026 the PSU marketers carried it first and the Government compensated later, partly. For the most marketing-heavy of them, the industry structure protects volumes and the network, not margins.

sections.title: Refining and marketing: one segment, two margin pools, and the political one is bigger

blocks.p: HPCL reports a single segment. Its EBITDA is the sum of a refining margin on ~26 MMT (GRM: product value less crude cost, US$/bbl), a marketing margin on ~51 MMT (retail price less the refinery-gate price, taxes and dealer commission), pipeline and terminal income and inventory gains or losses, less operating costs and exchange losses. HPCL reports its GRM every quarter but not the marketing margin; brokers back it out (PL: +₹6.3/litre in Q4FY26, −₹14.9/litre in Q1FY27).

blocks.h: Refining: Visakh is bigger and more complex; the upgrade still has to prove itself

blocks.p: The Visakh Refinery Modernisation lifted capacity from 8.3 to 15 MMTPA (throughput 8.4 MMT in FY22, 16.0 MMT in FY26), and the 3.55 MMTPA Residue Upgradation Facility (the world's first and largest LC-Max unit, converting ~93% of bottom-of-the-barrel residue into distillates; Nelson complexity 11.6) was commissioned in Dec-2025. It did not run stably in Q1FY27 (pressure, temperature and catalyst issues); management expects stability in Q2-Q3FY27 and BOB sees ~US$2.5/bbl more GRM at Visakh once it does. GRM was US$5.74/bbl in FY25 and US$8.79 in FY26 (Mumbai 8.04, Visakh 9.26), then US$23.8 in Q1FY27 before the export duty as diesel cracks reached ~US$50/bbl. In Mumbai a lube and bitumen upgrade (lube base oil 475 → 764 KTPA) is under way.

blocks.h: Marketing: volumes grow, margins are decided elsewhere

blocks.p: Marketing under-recoveries above ₹26,000 cr in Q1FY27: ~₹20,000 cr on petrol and diesel, the rest on domestic LPG. LPG under-recovery ₹510/cylinder on average in Q1, ₹680 in June, ~₹490 in July; July 'materially better'. The negative LPG buffer reached ₹16,410 cr at Jun-2026 even after ₹1,980 cr of compensation in the quarter. The Government cut excise by ₹10/litre in Mar-2026 and allowed price rises in tranches from May, and JPMorgan noted that petrol and diesel margins were back to pre-conflict levels by late June. HPCL is not compensated for petrol and diesel losses at all; it waits for crude to fall while prices are held.

blocks.callout: **Our forecast:** EBITDA of ₹3,674 / 23,243 / 25,054 cr (₹700 / 4300 / 4500 per tonne). FY27E assumes Q2-Q4 average ~₹5,000/t after Q1's −₹12,300/t. FY28-29E sit at the FY22-26 average without the FY23 loss year (₹4,300/t), with the residue upgrade and HRRL supply offsetting the risk of another squeeze. Each ₹500/t is ~₹2,703 cr of FY28E EBITDA (~₹9.5 of EPS).

sections.title: HRRL, HMEL and MRPL: ₹20,259 cr at book, with their debt outside HPCL's balance sheet

blocks.p: **HPCL Rajasthan Refinery (HRRL, 74%; Rajasthan 26%).** A 9 MMTPA refinery with 2.4 MMTPA of petrochemicals at Pachpadra, Barmer, the first integrated greenfield refinery-cum-petrochemical complex in India (26% petchem intensity). Approved at ₹43,129 cr, its cost was raised to ₹79,459 cr in Apr-2026 and HPCL's equity commitment to ₹19,600 cr. Crude went into the CDU in Feb-2026; commercial operation followed in end-June/July 2026 (dates differ by source). ~50-60% in Q2FY27, 80-85% in Q3FY27, full refinery capacity in Q4FY27; petrochemicals by end-FY27 (Q1 call via PL, Emkay). HPCL has invested ₹10,630 cr of equity (book ₹10,192 cr) and lent ₹8,286 cr as a subordinated loan to be converted into equity. If HPCL's ₹19,600 cr is 74% of the equity, total equity is ~₹26,500 cr and the rest of the cost (~₹53,000 cr, our estimate; HRRL's accounts are not published in what we read) is debt, which is not on HPCL's balance sheet. HRRL will add a refining and petchem margin through HPCL's share of JV profit and cut HPCL's third-party purchases; in the ramp-up its depreciation and interest will likely make it loss-making.

**HPCL-Mittal Energy (HMEL, 48.99%).** An 11.3 MMTPA refinery and petrochemicals at Bathinda, run with the Mittal group. Net assets ₹15,668 cr, net debt ~₹38,093 cr; profit ₹1,717 cr in FY26 after a ₹348 cr loss in FY25. HPCL bought ₹72,034 cr of product from it in FY26. **MRPL (16.96%)**, listed, 15 MMTPA at Mangalore, is ONGC's subsidiary; HPCL's 29.7 cr shares were worth ₹5,031 cr at the 30-Sep close.

blocks.callout: **So what:** the JVs are worth something, but probably less than their headline cost. HRRL took about twice its budget and four extra years; HMEL has swung between a ₹348 cr loss and a ₹1,717 cr profit. Carrying HRRL (equity and loan) and HMEL at book, rather than at zero like BOB and Emkay, adds ~₹123 a share to our value: a judgement in HPCL's favour.

sections.title: Competitive advantage: a dense network in the west and south, no pricing power; the moat protects volumes, not returns

verdicts: 25,098 fuel stations (third-largest), 6,389 LPG distributors (second-largest LPG marketer), pipelines and terminals; volumes grew faster than the industry in Q1FY27.
Retail prices set with the Government; Q1FY27 marketing under-recoveries above ₹26,000 cr; LPG losses compensated late and partly.
Returns cannot be defended in a spike; worst hit of the three OMCs.
Visakh at 11.6 Nelson complexity after the residue upgrade; 106% utilisation; GRMs historically below peers (PL).
Upgrade still has to run stably.
Own refineries cover ~half of sales; HRRL lifts JV cover to ~40% next year.
Better supply security; margin earned partly inside JVs.
State ownership brings LPG compensation and cheap funding, but price controls, windfall/export duties and directed capex.

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** HPCL has a valuable network and nobody will take its volumes. But a moat that does not let you set prices does not earn excess returns through the cycle: consolidated ROE was 18%, −19%, 40%, 14%, 31% in FY22-FY26, an average of ~17% that hides a loss year, and the next squeeze arrived within a quarter of the record.

sections.title: From a ₹7,192 cr EBITDA loss to a ₹30,645 cr profit in three years, and back to a loss in one quarter

blocks.p: HPCL's revenue follows the crude price (₹2.3 lakh cr in FY21, ₹4.4 lakh cr in FY23-FY26, net of excise), so revenue growth says little. What matters is the margin on each tonne it sells, and that swings with two things HPCL does not control: refining cracks and how far the Government lets retail prices follow crude. EBITDA was ₹10,244 cr in FY22, −₹7,192 cr in FY23 (retail prices held while crude spiked after the Ukraine war), ₹24,928 cr in FY24, ₹16,448 cr in FY25 (weak cracks, LPG losses) and a record ₹30,645 cr in FY26. Net profit went ₹7,294 → −6,980 → 16,015 → 6,736 → 18,047 cr. Because HPCL sells twice what it refines, a marketing squeeze hits it harder than IOC or BPCL: Q1FY27 alone lost ₹12,265 cr.

EBITDA margin: −1.6% to 7%; a 4-5% mid-cycle

blocks.callout: **Our view:** HPCL has no "normal" year to forecast from. Over FY22-FY26 EBITDA averaged ~₹3,100 per tonne sold (₹4,300 without the FY23 loss year; ₹5,300-6,000 in good years). We forecast ₹700/t for FY27E (Q1 was −₹12,300/t), then ₹4,300/t and ₹4,500/t: the five-year average without FY23, because the Vizag residue upgrade and HRRL supply should help, while the 2026 war showed again that marketing margins are a policy decision.

sections.title: Q1FY27: a ₹12,265 cr loss, the first in 14 quarters, as retail prices lagged US$100 crude

blocks.p: In the Jun-2026 quarter Brent averaged ~US$105/bbl (US$76 in Q4FY26) and retail prices rose only in tranches. Refining boomed (GRM US$23.8/bbl before the export duty, from US$3.1 a year earlier), but marketing lost far more: the implied marketing margin was −₹14.9/litre (PL), and under-recoveries topped ₹26,000 cr. Standalone EBITDA was −₹16,141 cr and the standalone loss ₹11,526 cr after a tax credit; the consolidated loss was ₹12,265 cr (EPS −₹57.64), with only ₹29 cr from the JVs. Inventory write-downs on crude deliberately stocked up to keep the refineries running added to the loss. Volumes held: throughput 6.5 MMT, sales 13.1 MMT (exports 0.88 MMT, +54% QoQ). Gross debt rose from ₹47,600 cr to ₹72,600 cr in the quarter.

sections.title: Capex of ₹10,000-14,000 cr a year plus ~₹19,000 cr into HRRL; ROE −23% to +31% with the cycle

blocks.p: Over FY24-FY26 HPCL generated ₹74,194 cr of operating cash and spent ₹27,979 cr on fixed assets (Screener's line; the company's own capex figure is higher, ₹10,223-11,270 cr a year standalone) and ₹7,765 cr on dividends; over FY21-FY23 ₹30,173 cr, ₹33,458 cr and ₹6,693 cr. The money went into the Visakh Refinery Modernisation (8.3 → 15 MMTPA) and its residue upgrade, the Mumbai expansion, pipelines, marketing and the Chhara LNG terminal; on top, HPCL has put ₹18,916 cr into HPCL Rajasthan Refinery (₹10,630 cr of equity and a ₹8,286 cr subordinated loan) of a ₹19,600 cr commitment. Management capped FY27 capex at ₹9,700 cr to protect the balance sheet. Returns follow the cycle: standalone ROE 32.5% in FY26, 16.9% in FY25 (AR), and a loss in FY23.

HRRL's cost nearly doubled to ₹79,459 cr and it carries ~₹53,000 cr of project debt off HPCL's balance sheet; whether it earns its cost of capital will decide whether that ₹19,600 cr was well spent.

sections.title: Earnings quality: inventory swings, an off-balance-sheet LPG buffer and JV debt

blocks.p: The accounts are audited by C&AG-appointed firms and are unqualified, but four items make reported profit a poor guide to the run-rate: (1) **inventory gains and losses**: HPCL carries ~₹40,000 cr of inventory (₹39,584 cr at Mar-26), so a sharp move in crude swings profit by thousands of crores (Q1FY27 had write-downs on deliberately high crude stocks); (2) **LPG compensation**: the ₹7,920 cr conveyed in Oct-2025 is booked in monthly instalments (₹3,300 cr in FY26) while the negative buffer (₹16,410 cr at Jun-2026) is not recognised; (3) **exchange losses** (₹2,490 cr in FY26 per PL) sit inside EBITDA; (4) **equity-accounted JVs**: HRRL, HMEL and MRPL reach the P&L as one line of "share of profit" (inside Screener's other income) while their debt (HRRL ~₹53,000 cr, HMEL ~₹38,100 cr net) stays off HPCL's balance sheet.

blocks.callout: **Our approach:** forecasts carry no inventory gains or losses and no exceptional items; FX losses and LPG compensation are inside our ₹/tonne margin; JV profits are in other income (₹500-1,200 cr a year as HRRL ramps up). Engine limit: the model books no tax credit on a loss (Q1 had a ₹5,905 cr credit), so we set the FY27E tax rate at 0% (keeping the report and the Excel model identical); FY27E net profit is ~₹1,400 cr worse than a 25% credit would give and Sep-27E net debt ~₹1,370 cr higher (~₹6 a share on the target).

sections.title: Net debt ~₹27,800 cr at Mar-26 after investments; gross debt +₹25,000 cr in Q1FY27

blocks.p: At Mar-2026 consolidated borrowings were ₹55,964 cr including ₹5,066 cr of leases, against ₹171 cr of cash and ₹28,012 cr of investments (HRRL ₹10,192 cr, HMEL ₹7,676 cr, MRPL ₹2,391 cr and other joint ventures ₹2,638 cr at equity value; Oil India ₹1,908 cr at fair value; ₹3,107 cr of government securities). Net of all investments, debt was ~₹27,800 cr, the lowest since FY19, after a strong FY26 (debt/equity 0.80x from 1.38x). It did not last: in Q1FY27 gross debt rose from ₹47,600 cr to ₹72,600 cr (debt/equity ~1.4-1.5x) as HPCL lost money and carried crude at war prices. Off balance sheet: a negative LPG buffer (under-recoveries not yet compensated) of ₹16,410 cr at Jun-2026, HRRL's project debt (~₹53,000 cr, 74% HPCL) and HMEL's net debt (~₹38,100 cr, 48.99%).

sections.title: Ownership: ONGC 54.9%; mutual funds and foreign funds ~36%; free float ~45%

blocks.p: ONGC owns 54.9% and has not sold since it bought the Government's stake in 2018; the Government controls HPCL through ONGC. Domestic institutions (mainly mutual funds) hold 22.85% and foreign funds 13.58% (Jun-2026; they had raised their stake to 17.3% in Mar-2026, then sold during the war); 5,18,531 shareholders hold the rest. The free float is ~45%. ONGC has no reason to sell, but HPCL's losses weigh on ONGC (the ONGC initiation treats HPCL as a listed stake at market less a holding discount).

blocks.p: Nine fundamental targets stood on 30-Sep-2026: six written after the Q1FY27 results on 22-Jul-2026 (Motilal Oswal Buy ₹470, ICICI Securities Buy ₹495, BOB Capital Hold ₹427, Emkay Add ₹410, Prabhudas Lilladher Reduce ₹350, Nomura Neutral ₹420) and three from before them (Kotak Reduce ₹400 in June, Geojit Hold ₹420 and Nuvama Reduce ₹372 in May). Median ₹420 (+20% vs the 30-Sep-2026 close of ₹350.4); the post-Q1 median is ₹424. Three of the four that disclose a method use 6x EV/EBITDA on standalone EBITDA (Dec-27E to Jun-28E) plus investments; PL uses 1.1x FY28E book. Targets fell through the year (MOSL ₹600 in Jan → 455 → 470; BOB ₹464 → 438 → 427; PL ₹427 in May → 386 → 350). Jefferies Underperform (raised from ₹275 after Q1): secondary reports disagree on the new target (₹315 vs ₹345) and none is clearly dated, so it is not counted. HDFC Securities Buy ₹579 (4-Feb-2026, 4.5x Mar-27E EV/EBITDA): written before the Gulf war; no later note found. InCred Hold ₹384: reported in a secondary summary without a verifiable date.

blocks.p: House rule (PLAYBOOK §4, §7c), as in our IOC initiation: start from the stock's own one-year-forward multiple from Apr-2021 to 30-Sep-2026, leave out trough years, then apply the sector's move against its five-year medians. Because the street values HPCL on EV/EBITDA plus investments, we measure the same thing: EV less ALL investments at their latest book value (so the stakes we add back are not counted twice), divided by the next full year's consolidated EBITDA (realised for past years, our FY27E-FY28E for recent dates), on every weekly close. Two forward years are troughs and left out: FY23 (an EBITDA loss of ₹7,192 cr) and FY27E (₹3,674 cr, below half of FY26's ₹30,645 cr). HPCL's history is badly distorted by these swings (weeks pricing FY23 show a median of -9.6x; weeks pricing FY27E 36.2x; weeks pricing FY24's record 2.5x), so we also show the median on a mid-cycle denominator and with the troughs kept, as sensitivity rows.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a good network carrying the most policy risk and the most debt of the OMCs; SELL

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** 25,098 fuel stations and India's second-largest LPG business, two refineries (24.5 MMTPA, Visakh newly upgraded), 74% of the just-started HRRL, 48.99% of HMEL, MRPL and Oil India stakes worth ₹6,831 cr, and ONGC as parent. EPS of ₹-25.7 / 48.9 / 55.5 in FY27-29E on our numbers.

**What you are paying:** ₹350.4 is 7.2x FY28E EPS and 4.4x FY28E core EBITDA (after taking out all investments at book). That is about the stock's own history (3.9x median, trough years out) and above it once the sector's discount to its averages is applied. Our 3.5x Sep-28E EBITDA (₹24,148 cr) gives {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): SELL. The street is more generous (median ₹420) because it pays 6x EBITDA and adds investments on top.

bullets: **Rating: SELL, target {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}).** Our ratings follow the upside to our 12−month target: BUY at +15% or more, HOLD between −5% and +15%, SELL below −5%.
**We would move to HOLD if the price fell below ~₹321**, and to BUY below ~₹265, on today's numbers.

**This is a multiple and leverage call, not an earnings call.** Our FY28E EBITDA (₹23,243 cr) is inside the street's range (₹21,700-25,300 cr). Each 0.5x on the EV/EBITDA multiple is ~₹57 a share; the bull multiple (4x, no sector move) with stakes at market gives {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}.

**What would change our mind:** evidence that marketing margins are protected in this cycle (prices that follow crude, LPG compensation on time), HRRL running profitably, or a material fall in the price.
